### Erdbeschreibung: *Columbia* (London, 1822), Fortsetzung

_[From a review in the Allgemeine Literatur-Zeitung (Halle), January 1834, nos. 16–17, of the English compilation Colombia: Being a Geographical, Statistical, Agricultural, Commercial and Political Account of That Country (London: Baldwin, Cradock & Joy, 1822). The Fraktur OCR of this page is very poor. The passage below is reconstructed by hand with spelling normalised (ſ as s); words in [square brackets] are conjectural, and the whole needs checking against the page images.]_
transcript_text:
Ein anderes eigenthümliches Nahrungsmittel der Missionen am Niederorinoco ist die Gewinnung der Schildkröteneyer, welche die Arrau-Schildkröte im Sande am Ufer zur Zeit des niedrigsten Wasserstandes vergräbt. Sie legt solche in der Nacht. Die Mönche der Missionen, jetzt Franciscaner, vorher Jesuiten, halten hier treffliche Polizey, dass die Eyer beym Ausgraben nicht beschädigt werden, aber die Ärndte nimmt mit jedem Jahre ab. […] Das Ufer der Uruana liefert allein 1000 Botijas solchen Öls, zu 2 bis [3] Piaster. […]

Affenfleisch und Eidechsen helfen die Indianer mit ernähren. Das Hauptgetränke derselben am Orinoco ist Palmwein von der Sagopalme. In der Periode, da dieser gewonnen wird, werden die ihn stark geniessenden Indianer fetter. Auch von Cassava und Mays brauen sie Getränke und **berauschen sich durch die Dämpfe des Niopopulvers, welches starkes Niesen veranlasst. Niopo (Acacia) ist eine baumartige Tabakspflanze vom Geschlecht der Mimosen.** Die [Otomaken] und die Omaguas geniessen viel Federharz oder verdickte Milch der Euphorbien und Nesseln. Den krautartigen Orinocotabak rauchte man bereits, als die Spanier in Südamerica landeten. Sie wickelten Maysblätter um ihre Cigarren und kannten die narkotische Kraft desselben ([mit offenen Augen zu schlafen]) sehr wohl. Jetzt raucht der Indianer in den Missionen und auch der Creole wenig. Gekauet wird der Tabak auf dem Festlande nirgends. Der Tabak gedeiht wild in mässiger Gebirgstemperatur der Tropen. Europa empfing den ersten Tabakssaamen 1559 aus der mexicanischen Provinz Yucatan. **Wenn die Indianer berauscht sind, üben sie besinnungslos oft Mordthaten, welches die Missionarien nicht zu verhindern vermögen.**

### Geography: *Colombia* (London, 1822), continued

_[Machine-assisted translation of the reconstructed German above; conjectural readings remain in brackets.]_

Another peculiar food of the missions on the lower Orinoco is the harvest of turtle eggs, which the arrau turtle buries in the sand of the bank at the time of lowest water. It lays them at night. The monks of the missions, now Franciscans, formerly Jesuits, keep excellent order here so that the eggs are not damaged in digging them up, but the harvest diminishes every year. […] The bank at Uruana alone yields 1,000 *botijas* of such oil, at 2 to [3] piastres. […]

Monkey flesh and lizards help to feed the Indians. Their chief drink on the Orinoco is palm wine from the sago palm; in the season when it is made, the Indians who drink a great deal of it grow fatter. They also brew drinks from cassava and maize, and **intoxicate themselves with the fumes of niopo powder, which causes violent sneezing. Niopo (*Acacia*) is a tree-like tobacco plant of the mimosa family.** The [Otomac] and the Omagua consume much rubber, or the thickened milk of euphorbias and nettles. The herbaceous Orinoco tobacco was already smoked when the Spaniards landed in South America; they wrapped maize leaves around their cigars and knew its narcotic power ([to sleep with open eyes]) very well. Now the Indian in the missions, and the Creole too, smokes little. Tobacco is chewed nowhere on the mainland. It grows wild in the moderate mountain temperatures of the tropics. Europe received the first tobacco seed in 1559 from the Mexican province of Yucatán. **When the Indians are intoxicated they often commit murders senselessly, which the missionaries are unable to prevent.**

fields.title: Niopo on the Orinoco, in a German review of Colombia (1822)
fields.subtitle: Allgemeine Literatur-Zeitung, January 1834: review of Colombia (London, 1822)
fields.summary: A long German review of an English compendium on Gran Colombia summarises its account of the Indigenous peoples of the Orinoco missions: turtle-egg oil at Uruana, palm wine and cassava beer. It also records niopo, a powder whose fumes intoxicate and cause violent sneezing, and that intoxicated men commit murders the missionaries cannot prevent. The material ultimately derives from Alexander von Humboldt's account of the Otomac. It shows that information circulated third-hand, from Humboldt to an English compilation to a German review.
fields.citation: Review of *Colombia: Being a Geographical, Statistical, Agricultural, Commercial and Political Account of That Country* (London: Baldwin, Cradock & Joy, 1822), *Allgemeine Literatur-Zeitung* (Halle), January 1834, nos. 16–17.

editor_notes: DATE CORRECTED: Common Corpus gives 1785, the journal's founding year; the page itself is January 1834. This is a third-hand echo of Humboldt (Personal Narrative, ch. 24), so its main value is showing how the information circulated. I would decline it in favour of tracing Humboldt's own text, which the Humboldt proposal in this batch also points to.
